inflation-costs-s1.title: A one-year loan in Country X
inflation-costs-s1.text: Maya borrows \$10,000 from a credit union for one year at a fixed interest rate of 8%, so she will repay \$10,800. When they sign, both Maya and the credit union believe inflation over the year will be about 3%. In fact prices rise 8% over the year: the consumer price index goes from 100 to 108.

inflation-costs-s2.title: A surprise jump in inflation in Country Q
inflation-costs-s2.text: For years, inflation in Country Q was about 2%, and everyone planned on that. This year it jumps to 9%. Four people react: Ruth is retired and lives on a pension of the same dollar amount every month. Dev has a union contract that raises his pay each year by the rise in the CPI. Lucia owns a restaurant and has reprinted her menus twice to show higher prices. Tom now keeps less cash in his wallet and goes to the bank more often, so his money does not sit losing value.

inflation-costs-s3.title: A savings account and inflation in Country Z

table.caption: A savings account in Country Z that pays a fixed 3% interest each year (invented data for practice)

items.q: Who gains from the inflation in this scenario?
options: Maya, the borrower
The credit union, the lender
Both gain, because the interest rate was fixed
Neither, because the loan is repaid in full

why.correct: Unanticipated inflation helps borrowers with fixed-rate loans and hurts lenders: the money paid back buys less than either side expected when they signed.
options: Right: inflation was higher than both sides planned, so she repays with dollars that buy less than the dollars she borrowed.
The lender is repaid in dollars worth less than it planned on, so it loses.
A fixed rate is exactly why the surprise moves purchasing power from one side to the other.
The dollar amount is repaid, but those dollars buy less than both sides planned.

items.q: Measured in the prices of the day Maya borrowed, how much is her \$10,800 repayment worth, in dollars?

why.correct: Divide by the price index and multiply by 100: $\frac{10{,}800}{108} \times 100 = 10{,}000$ dollars. The credit union gets back no more purchasing power than it lent.

mistakes.why: That is the dollar amount repaid. Prices rose 8%, so divide by the index: $\frac{10{,}800}{108} \times 100$.
You multiplied by the index. Higher prices make the repayment worth less, so divide by the index.

items.q: Suppose instead that prices had risen only 1% over the year. Who would have gained compared with what both sides planned?
options: The credit union: repaid dollars buy more than planned
Maya, because her interest rate was fixed for the whole year
Neither side, because inflation was positive
Both sides equally, because prices rose a little

why.correct: The surprise runs both ways. Lower-than-anticipated inflation helps lenders and savers and hurts fixed-rate borrowers.
options: Right: inflation below what both sides planned on helps the lender and hurts the fixed-rate borrower.
With inflation lower than planned, each dollar she repays is worth more, so the fixed rate costs her more.
What matters is the surprise: actual inflation of 1% versus the 3% both planned on.
A surprise moves purchasing power from one side to the other; it cannot help both.

items.q: Why would the loan have redistributed little if both sides had correctly anticipated 8% inflation?
options: They would have agreed on a higher interest rate
Anticipated inflation does not raise prices
Borrowing is not allowed when inflation is high
The credit union would have refused to lend at a fixed rate

why.correct: Anticipated inflation is priced into contracts. It is the unanticipated part that moves purchasing power between borrowers and lenders.
options: Right: when inflation is anticipated, lenders build it into the interest rate, so the borrower pays back enough to keep the lender's purchasing power.
Anticipated inflation raises prices just as much; people simply plan for it.
Nothing stops lending during inflation; the rate is set to allow for it.
Lenders can lend at a fixed rate if it includes the inflation they anticipate.

items.q: How does the jump in inflation affect Ruth?
options: She is hurt: her pension buys less
She gains, because her pension stays the same
She is unaffected, because she is retired
She gains, because retirees spend less

why.correct: People on fixed incomes, such as a pension that does not rise with prices, lose purchasing power when inflation is higher than planned.
options: Right: a fixed income in dollars loses purchasing power when prices rise faster than planned.
The same dollars buy fewer goods when prices rise, so she can afford less.
Retirees still buy goods and services, so rising prices matter to them.
Spending less does not protect a fixed income from rising prices.

items.q: How does the jump in inflation affect Dev?
options: He is roughly protected: his pay follows the CPI
He is hurt badly, because inflation rose to 9%
He gains a lot, because his pay rises 9%
He is hurt, because union contracts are fixed in dollars

why.correct: Indexing, a cost-of-living adjustment tied to a price index, protects incomes from inflation.
options: Right: indexing his pay to the CPI keeps his purchasing power about the same.
His raise follows the CPI, so his pay keeps up with prices.
His pay rises about as fast as prices, so his purchasing power barely changes.
This contract is tied to the CPI, not fixed in dollars.

items.q: Lucia reprinting her menus is an example of which cost of inflation?
options: Menu costs
Shoe-leather costs
Substitution bias
Unemployment costs

why.correct: Menu costs are the real resources used to change prices. They rise with how often prices must change.
options: Right: the cost of changing posted prices, such as printing menus or updating price tags and websites.
Shoe-leather costs are the time and effort of holding less cash, as Tom does.
Substitution bias is a measurement problem with the CPI, not a cost to a firm.
Lucia keeps her restaurant open; the cost here is updating prices.

items.q: Tom keeping less cash and making more trips to the bank is an example of which cost of inflation?
options: Shoe-leather costs
Menu costs
A fixed-income loss
Deflation

why.correct: Inflation makes cash lose purchasing power, so people hold less of it and spend time and effort managing their money.
options: Right: the time and effort of holding less cash so it does not lose value, named for wearing out shoes on trips to the bank.
Menu costs are a seller's costs of changing prices.
Tom is changing how he holds money, not living on a fixed payment.
Prices are rising, not falling.

items.q: In which year does the saver's account buy less at the end of the year than at the start?
options: Year 3
Year 1
Year 2
Each year, because inflation is above zero

why.correct: Savings lose purchasing power when inflation is higher than the interest they earn.
options: Right: prices rose 5% while the account grew 3%, so the balance buys about 2% less.
The balance grew 3% while prices rose 1%, so it buys more.
The balance and prices both rose 3%, so its purchasing power stayed about the same.
The balance keeps up with prices when its interest is at least as high as inflation.

items.q: In Year 2, what happens to the purchasing power of the savings?
options: It stays about the same
It rises 3%
It falls 3%
It rises 6%

why.correct: Compare the interest earned with the inflation rate: equal rates leave purchasing power unchanged.
options: Right: the balance grows 3% and prices rise 3%, so it buys about the same amount.
The balance rises 3% in dollars, but prices rose 3% too.
The interest earned keeps the balance even with prices.
Price increases reduce purchasing power; they are not added to the interest.

items.q: The bank set the 3% rate when it anticipated inflation of about 1%. Who gains in Year 3?
options: The bank, which borrows from its savers at a fixed rate
The saver, because the interest rate is fixed
Both, because the account still grows
Neither, because the rate is set by the bank

why.correct: A deposit is a loan from the saver to the bank. When inflation turns out higher than anticipated, the borrower (the bank) gains and the lender (the saver) loses.
options: Right: a saver lends to the bank. Inflation above what the bank anticipated means it repays savers in dollars worth less.
The fixed rate is below inflation in Year 3, so the saver loses purchasing power.
The account grows in dollars, but less than prices; the bank, as borrower, is the one that gains.
Who sets the rate does not matter; the surprise in inflation does.

items.q: Prices unexpectedly fall 2% in a year. Who is hurt?
options: People repaying fixed-rate loans
Lenders receiving fixed payments
People on fixed pensions
Savers earning a fixed interest rate

why.correct: Unanticipated deflation reverses the effects of unanticipated inflation: lenders and fixed-income earners gain, fixed-rate borrowers lose.
options: Right: with deflation the dollars they repay buy more than the dollars they borrowed, so the burden of the debt grows.
Deflation makes the dollars they receive worth more, so lenders gain.
A fixed pension buys more when prices fall.
Their savings buy more as prices fall, so savers gain.

items.q: Which costs of inflation occur even when everyone anticipates it correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Menu costs of changing prices often
Shoe-leather costs of holding less cash
A transfer of purchasing power from lenders to borrowers
Losses to people whose pensions rise with the CPI

why.correct: Menu and shoe-leather costs come with any inflation. The redistribution between borrowers and lenders comes from the unanticipated part.
options: Right: prices must still be changed, even when everyone planned on it.
Right: cash still loses value, so people still hold less of it.
When inflation is anticipated, it is built into interest rates, so the transfer happens only when inflation is a surprise.
An indexed pension keeps up with prices, so its owner is protected.

items.q: Which is an example of a fixed income?
options: A pension that pays the same dollar amount every month
A wage that rises each year by the rise in the CPI
Profits from a business whose prices rise with inflation
A salary renegotiated each year to match prices

why.correct: A fixed income is a set number of dollars, so its purchasing power falls when prices rise.
options: Right: its dollar amount does not change when prices rise.
That income is indexed to prices, so it is not fixed in purchasing power or in dollars.
Business income can rise as the firm raises its prices.
A salary that is adjusted to prices is not fixed.

items.q: A bank makes 30-year home loans at a fixed interest rate. Inflation then turns out far higher than the bank anticipated. Which statement best describes the result?
options: Homeowners repay in dollars worth less, so the bank loses
The bank gains, because homeowners have to pay more interest
Neither side is affected, because the rate was agreed to in advance
Homeowners lose, because house prices rise with inflation

why.correct: Long fixed-rate contracts are where unanticipated inflation moves the most purchasing power. That risk is one reason lenders also offer adjustable rates.
options: Right: fixed-rate borrowers gain and the lender loses when inflation is higher than anticipated.
The rate is fixed, so homeowners pay the same dollar interest, which now buys less.
Agreeing in advance is what exposes both sides to the surprise.
Rising house prices add to homeowners' wealth; the fixed payments get easier, not harder.

items.q: Why does high, unpredictable inflation make it harder for a firm to plan a new factory?
options: The firm can't tell what future costs and prices will be
Inflation makes factories illegal to build
Inflation lowers the number of workers in the labor force
Factories are not counted in GDP during inflation

why.correct: Uncertainty is a cost of inflation: when people cannot predict prices, they hesitate to sign long contracts or make long-lived investments.
options: Right: uncertainty about inflation makes long-term contracts and plans riskier.
No such rule exists; the problem is uncertainty about future prices.
Inflation itself does not shrink the labor force.
A new factory is investment in GDP whatever the inflation rate.
